content: Endometrial adenocarcinoma is a prevalent type of gynecological cancer, but only a small percentage of patients present with or develop advanced or recurrent disease. For those who do experience disease progression or recurrence, the prognosis is generally poor, and the most effective treatment approach remains uncertain. Factors such as co-existing medical conditions, including obesity and cardiac disease, as well as concerns about the toxicity of treatments, have limited the scope of research into cytotoxic chemotherapy, despite the availability of several active agents. The objective of this study was to evaluate the potential benefits and adverse effects of cytotoxic chemotherapy in women diagnosed with advanced, recurrent, or metastatic endometrial adenocarcinoma. To achieve this, systematic searches were conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, CENTRAL, and the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer specialist trials register, covering studies from 1966 to January 2012. Additional searches were performed in relevant trial registries and conference proceedings to ensure comprehensive data collection. The review focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared chemotherapy with other interventions, including different chemotherapy regimens, in cases of advanced disease. Trials involving adjuvant treatments or sarcomatous tumors were excluded. Data extraction was performed by the review authors, and further information was sought from the authors of the included studies. Fourteen eligible trials were identified, with patient recruitment spanning from 1974 to 2005. Among these, eight trials specifically compared more-intensive chemotherapy regimens with less-intensive ones. These eight trials, which included a total of 1,519 patients, demonstrated that more-intensive chemotherapy was associated with improved overall survival (OS) (hazard ratio [HR] 0.86; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.77 to 0.96; P = 0.005) and longer progression-free survival (PFS) (HR 0.82; 95% CI 0.74 to 0.90; P < 0.0001). However, these more-intensive regimens were also linked to a higher incidence of serious acute toxicities. The analysis did not provide evidence to suggest that any specific doublet chemotherapy regimen was superior or inferior to another, nor that any single-agent chemotherapy was better or worse than another. However, the data available for these comparisons were limited. Additionally, no trials were identified that directly compared chemotherapy with endocrine therapy or best supportive care alone. The authors concluded that more-intensive chemotherapy regimens may offer improvements in both overall survival and progression-free survival for women with advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer. However, due to inconsistencies in the cytotoxic drug combinations evaluated in the randomized trials conducted thus far, the optimal chemotherapy regimen has yet to be determined. Future clinical trials should incorporate assessments of quality of life (QoL) and symptom control in addition to survival and disease progression outcomes.
